ap_calculus_ab-m01.stem: The function $f$ is continuous on $[0,8]$ and $f(0)=1$. The graph of $f'$ is shown and consists of line segments. What is the absolute maximum value of $f$ on $[0,8]$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f', consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Reports f(6), the value at the relative minimum.
Reports the x-coordinate of the relative maximum, 2, instead of a value of f.
Reports f(2), the value at the relative maximum, without comparing it with the endpoint value f(8).
The candidates are the endpoints and the critical points; f is evaluated at each using f(0) plus the signed area under f', and the largest value is chosen.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find an absolute maximum from the graph of f' using the candidates test and net area
student_thinking: Find the critical points from the zeros of f' and classify them by sign change
Compute f at each candidate and endpoint using f(0) plus the signed area under f'
Compare the candidate values

key_conditions.condition: f is continuous on a closed interval so an absolute maximum exists and occurs at an endpoint or a critical point
key_conditions.evidence: Extreme Value Theorem applies on [0, 8]

verification.independent_path: numerical integration of f' to every grid point and maximum of f over a 0.25 grid (independent of the candidate comparison)

ap_calculus_ab-m02.stem: The graph of the function $f$ is shown and consists of line segments. Let $g(x)=\int_x^{10} f(t)\,dt$ for $0\le x\le 10$. At which value of $x$ does $g$ have a relative maximum?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: g'(x) = -f(x) because x is the lower limit; g' changes from positive to negative where f changes from negative to positive.
Chooses x = 4, a vertex of the graph, without checking the sign change of f.
Treats the zero where f changes from positive to negative as the maximum, forgetting that g'(x) = -f(x) because x is the lower limit.
Chooses x = 6, a vertex of the graph, without checking the sign change of f.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Locate a relative extremum of an accumulation function whose variable is the lower limit
student_thinking: Apply the Fundamental Theorem with the variable lower limit: g' = -f
Find where g' changes from positive to negative, i.e. where f changes from negative to positive
Read that zero from the graph of f

key_conditions.condition: g is differentiable with g'(x) = -f(x) because f is continuous
key_conditions.evidence: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with a variable lower limit

misconceptions.description: chooses the + to - crossing of f
picks a vertex without a sign change
chooses a vertex because f is large or small there

verification.independent_path: g computed by numerical quadrature on a fine grid and its relative maximum located by comparing neighbouring values (independent of the sign analysis)

ap_calculus_ab-m03.stem: The graphs of the functions $f$ and $g$ are shown, each consisting of line segments. The graphs cross at least once between $x=0$ and $x=8$. What is the total area of the region enclosed between the two graphs for $0\le x\le 8$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of f and g, each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Uses the absolute value of the net integral, |integral of (f - g)|.
Integrates f - g over the whole interval, so the area below the crossing cancels the area above it.
Reports the area under the graph of f alone.
The area is the integral of |f - g|: the graphs cross, so the upper and lower functions switch and each piece must be counted as positive.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Set up and evaluate the area between two graphs that cross
student_thinking: Identify where the graphs cross and which one is above on each piece
Integrate (upper - lower) on each piece using areas read from the graphs
Add the positive piece areas

key_conditions.condition: area between curves is the integral of the absolute difference when the curves cross
key_conditions.evidence: definition of area between curves

misconceptions.description: takes the absolute value of the net

verification.independent_path: numerical quadrature of |f - g| with breakpoints at the vertices (independent of the exact crossing computation)

ap_calculus_ab-m04.stem: The figure shows the graph of $f(x)=4\sin x$ and the line $L$. Let $R$ be the region enclosed by the graph of $f$ and the line $L$. What is the area of $R$?

stimulus.description: Graph of the curve y = f(x) and the line L; the region R between them is described in the problem.

options.why: Computes the area under the line alone between the intersection points.
The line is read from the graph; the two intersection points are found with a calculator and the area is the integral of f - L between them.
Computes the area under the curve alone between the intersection points.
Integrates over the whole interval 0 to 4 instead of between the two intersection points.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find the area between a curve given by a formula and a line given only by a graph
student_thinking: Read two lattice points on the line from the figure and write its equation
Find the two intersection points of the curve and the line with a calculator
Integrate (curve - line) between the intersection points

key_conditions.condition: f is above L between the two intersection points
key_conditions.evidence: shown in the figure

must_include: line L through two lattice points

verification.independent_path: composite Simpson rule on f - L between roots recomputed by Brent's method (independent of scipy quad)

ap_calculus_ab-m05.stem: The graph of the function $f$, which consists of line segments, is shown. What is the average rate of change of $f$ on the interval $[4,8]$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Average rate of change = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a), with both values read from the graph.
Reports the change f(b) - f(a) without dividing by the length of the interval.
Uses the slope of the segment that ends at x = 8 instead of the change over the whole interval.
Averages the two endpoint values f(a) and f(b) instead of the change in f.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Compute an average rate of change over an interval from the graph of a piecewise linear function
student_thinking: Read f(a) and f(b) from the graph
Form the difference quotient over the interval

key_conditions.condition: average rate of change is the change in f divided by the change in x
key_conditions.evidence: definition, stated by the question

misconceptions.description: uses only the final segment slope

verification.independent_path: quadrature of the piecewise slope function over [a, b] divided by b - a (independent of f(b) - f(a))

ap_calculus_ab-m06.stem: The graph of the function $f$ on $[0,8]$ is shown and consists of line segments. What is the average value of $f$ on the interval $[0,8]$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Averages the five vertex values read from the graph instead of integrating.
Average value = (1/(b - a)) times the integral of f over [a, b]; the integral is the signed area read from the graph.
Reports the integral of f over [0, 8] and does not divide by the length of the interval.
Divides the integral by 4, the number of line segments, instead of by the interval length 8.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Compute the average value of a function from its graph as integral divided by interval length
student_thinking: Compute the signed area under the graph from 0 to 8
Divide by the interval length 8

key_conditions.condition: the average value of a continuous function on [a, b] is the integral divided by b - a
key_conditions.evidence: definition (mean value of a function)

misconceptions.description: divides by the number of segments

verification.independent_path: numerical quadrature of the interpolated graph divided by 8 (independent of trapezoid areas)

ap_calculus_ab-m07.stem: Let $f(x)=\sin\left(\frac{x^{2}}{10}\right)+1$, and let $g$ be the function whose graph, consisting of line segments, is shown for $0\le x\le 8$. What is the average value of $f(x)+g(x)$ on the interval $[0,8]$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Averages only f and ignores g.
Average value = (1/8)(integral of f + integral of g); the integral of f needs a calculator and the integral of g is the area read from the graph.
Averages only g and ignores f.
Reports the integral of f + g over [0, 8] and does not divide by the interval length.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find the average value of a sum of a formula and a graphed function
student_thinking: Write the average value as (1/(b - a)) times the integral over [a, b]
Evaluate the integral of f with a calculator and the integral of g from the graph
Divide the combined integral by the interval length

key_conditions.condition: the average value of a continuous function on [a, b] is the integral divided by b - a
key_conditions.evidence: definition of average value

verification.independent_path: composite Simpson rule (20001 nodes) on f + g with g interpolated, divided by 8 (independent of the split into two integrals)

ap_calculus_ab-m08.stem: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x^{2}+5}$, and let $g$ be the function whose graph, consisting of line segments, is shown. If $h(x)=f(g(x))$, what is the value of $h'(3)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Reports f'(g(a)) and leaves out the inner derivative g'(a).
h'(a) = f'(g(a)) g'(a): g(a) and the slope g'(a) are read from the graph, f' is evaluated at g(a) with a calculator.
Uses the value f(g(a)) in place of the derivative f'(g(a)).
Evaluates f' at x = 3 instead of at the inner value g(3).

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Apply the chain rule at a point with a formula for the outer function and a graph for the inner function
student_thinking: Read g(a) and g'(a) from the graph
Differentiate f and evaluate f'(g(a)) numerically with a calculator
Multiply f'(g(a)) by g'(a)

key_conditions.condition: g is differentiable at x = a because a is interior to a segment; f is differentiable everywhere
key_conditions.evidence: a is odd and vertices of g are at even x

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of f(g(x)) with f lambdified and g interpolated (independent of the chain rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m09.stem: The graphs of $f$ and $g$ are shown, and each consists of line segments. Let $h(x)=f(g(x))$. What is the value of $h'(5)$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of f and g, each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Uses f(g(a)) in place of the derivative f'(g(a)).
Reports f'(g(a)) and omits the inner derivative factor g'(a).
Adds f'(g(a)) and g'(a) instead of multiplying them.
h'(a) = f'(g(a)) g'(a): g(a) is read from the graph of g, then the slope of f at that input is multiplied by the slope of g.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Apply the chain rule to a composition of two functions given by graphs
student_thinking: Read g(a) and g'(a) from the graph of g
Find the slope of f at the input g(a) from the graph of f
Multiply f'(g(a)) by g'(a)

key_conditions.condition: g(a) and a are interior to line segments of g and f so both derivatives exist
key_conditions.evidence: g(a) is an odd integer and a is an odd integer, never a vertex

misconceptions.description: evaluates f' at a instead of g(a)

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of the numerically composed interpolants (independent of the chain rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m10.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)$ equal to the graph shown for $0\le x\le 2$ and $f(x)=k\ln(x+1)+1$ for $2<x\le 5$, where $k$ is a constant. For what value of $k$ is $f$ continuous at $x=2$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f for 0 <= x <= 2, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Divides by 3 instead of ln 3: treats ln(x + 1) at x = 2 as 3.
Continuity at 2 requires the right-hand limit k ln 3 + 1 to equal f(2) = 6 read from the graph, so k = (6 - 1)/ln 3 (calculator).
Equates the slopes instead of the values at x = 2.
Forgets the constant 1 in the right-hand piece: k = f(2)/ln 3.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Choose a constant that makes a function continuous where one piece is a graph and the other a formula
student_thinking: Read f(2) from the graph of the left piece
Set the right-hand limit k ln 3 + c equal to f(2)
Solve for k with a calculator

key_conditions.condition: continuity at 2 requires the left piece value, the right-hand limit and f(2) to agree
key_conditions.evidence: definition of continuity at a point

verification.independent_path: k substituted back into the right-hand piece and compared with the plotted value f(2) (independent of the algebra for k)

ap_calculus_ab-m11.stem: The graph of the function $f$ is shown. At which value of $x=c$ does $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist while $f$ is not continuous at $x=c$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f on [0, 8]: four line segments with open and filled circles at x = 2, 4, 6 and one separate filled point.

options.why: The graph has a jump at x = 6: the left and right limits differ, so the limit does not exist.
At the corner x = 2 the limit equals the function value, so f is continuous there; the corner affects differentiability, not continuity.
At x = 4 both sides approach the same value (the open circles coincide) but the plotted point f(4) is elsewhere, so the limit exists and f is not continuous there.
x = 3 is in the middle of a segment, where the limit exists and equals f(3), so f is continuous there.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Classify points of a graph by limit existence and continuity
student_thinking: Compare the left and right limits at each candidate point
Compare the common limit with the plotted function value
Select the point where the limit exists but the function value is different

key_conditions.condition: continuity at c requires the limit to exist and equal f(c)
key_conditions.evidence: definition of continuity at a point

must_include: a separate filled point at the removable discontinuity

misconceptions.description: limit does not exist at a jump
a regular interior point is continuous

verification.independent_path: side limits and function values compared numerically from the plotted piece endpoints (independent of how the picture types were assigned)

ap_calculus_ab-m12.stem: The graph of the function $f$ is shown on the interval $0\le x\le 8$. It consists of line segments. For how many values of $x$ in the open interval $(0,8)$ is $f$ not differentiable?

stimulus.description: Graph of f: line segments with a jump (open and filled circles) at x = 2.

options.why: Counts only the corners and forgets that f is not even continuous at x = 2.
f is not differentiable at the discontinuity (x = 2) and at each corner where the slope changes (1 of them); a vertex where the two slopes are equal is differentiable.
Counts every vertex including the discontinuity twice, once as a break and once as a corner.
Counts every vertex of the graph in (0, 8) as a point where f is not differentiable, including the vertex where the two slopes agree.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Count points of non-differentiability from a graph with a discontinuity and corners
student_thinking: Recognize that a jump discontinuity prevents differentiability
At each continuous vertex compare the slopes on both sides to detect corners
Add the discontinuity and the corners

key_conditions.condition: a function is differentiable at a point only if it is continuous there and the one-sided slopes agree
key_conditions.evidence: theorem connecting differentiability and continuity

must_include: an open circle and a filled point at the discontinuity

verification.independent_path: numerical one-sided difference slopes and one-sided values around each interior vertex on the plotted pieces (independent of the vertex slope list)

ap_calculus_ab-m13.stem: The graph of $f'$, the derivative of $f$, is shown for $0\le x\le 6$ and consists of line segments. Let $g(x)=3xe^{-x/3}$ and $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)$. At what value of $x$ in $(0,6)$ is $h'(x)=0$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f', consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Solves f'(x) = g(x) instead of f'(x) = g'(x).
h'(x) = f'(x) - g'(x) = 0; f' is read from the graph (linear on each segment) and g' from the formula, and the equation is solved with a calculator.
Finds where f'(x) = 0 on the graph and ignores the term from g.
Takes the midpoint of the interval, x = 3.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find a critical point of a difference of a function known by its derivative graph and a formula
student_thinking: Write h' = f' - g' and set it equal to zero
Use the graph of f' (linear on each segment) and the derivative of g from the formula
Solve the equation numerically with a calculator

key_conditions.condition: h is differentiable on (0, 6) and has exactly one critical point
key_conditions.evidence: the difference f' - g' changes sign exactly once on the interval for the plotted graph

misconceptions.description: uses g in place of g'

verification.independent_path: bisection with 80 halvings on f'(x) - g'(x) using numerically interpolated f' and sympy g' (independent of Brent's method)

ap_calculus_ab-m14.stem: A population $P$ at time $t$ (in years) satisfies the differential equation $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP$ for a constant $k$. The graph of $P$ is shown and passes through the labeled points $A$ and $B$. What is the value of $k$?

stimulus.description: Graph of P(t), an increasing exponential curve, with labeled points A and B.

options.why: Takes ln of the value P(2) = 8 instead of the ratio P(2)/P(0), then divides by 2.
P(t) = P(0) e^{kt}; the labeled points give P(2) / P(0) = 4, so k = ln(4)/2.
Divides the ratio by the time, 4/2, without taking the logarithm.
Takes ln of the ratio but forgets to divide by the elapsed time 2.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find the growth constant of an exponential model from two points on its graph
student_thinking: Read the coordinates of the labeled points A and B from the graph
Use P(t) = P(0) e^{kt} to relate the ratio of values to the exponent
Solve for k using a natural logarithm

key_conditions.condition: solutions of dP/dt = kP have the form P(0) e^{kt}
key_conditions.evidence: exponential model stated in the problem

must_include: labeled points A = (0, P0) and B = (T, m P0)

misconceptions.description: ln of the ratio without dividing by t
uses the average rate of change
ln of the value instead of the ratio

verification.independent_path: k recomputed as ln(P(T)/P(0))/T from the dense numerical curve samples (independent of the exact exponents)

ap_calculus_ab-m15.stem: A quantity $P$ at time $t$ (in years) satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP$. The graph of $P$ for $0\le t\le 4$ is shown and passes through the labeled points $A$ and $B$. What is the value of $P(5)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of P(t), an increasing exponential curve, with labeled points A and B.

options.why: Uses k = ln(m)/T but starts from P(2) instead of P(0).
From the labeled points, P(2)/P(0) = 2, so k = ln(2)/2; then P(5) = P(0) e^{5 k} evaluated with a calculator.
Multiplies P(2) by the ratio once per year instead of per 2 years: P(0) m^{t}.
Extends the chord slope linearly: P(0) + (P(2) - P(0))/2 times 5.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Use an exponential model read from two points on a graph to find a later value
student_thinking: Read the labeled points A and B from the graph
Find k from P(T)/P(0) = e^{kT}
Evaluate P(t) = P(0) e^{kt} at a later time with a calculator

key_conditions.condition: solutions of dP/dt = kP have the form P(0) e^{kt}
key_conditions.evidence: exponential model stated in the problem

must_include: labeled points A = (0, P0) and B = (2, m P0)

misconceptions.description: uses ln m without dividing by T

verification.independent_path: P(t1) recomputed as P(0) (P(T)/P(0))^(t1/T) (independent of the exponent k)

ap_calculus_ab-m16.stem: The graph of $f'$, the derivative of a function $f$, is shown and consists of line segments. On which of the following intervals is $f$ increasing and concave down?

stimulus.description: Graph of f', consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: On (0, 2) f' is positive and increasing, so f is increasing but concave up, not concave down.
On (6, 8) f' is negative, so f is decreasing there; f' increasing makes f concave up.
f' is positive (f increasing) and f' is decreasing (f concave down) on this interval.
On (4, 6) f' is negative and decreasing, so f is decreasing and concave down; it is not increasing.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Connect the sign and the slope of the graph of f' to monotonicity and concavity of f
student_thinking: f is increasing where f' is positive
f is concave down where f' is decreasing
Find the interval satisfying both conditions

key_conditions.condition: f' is linear on each interval so its sign and its direction do not change inside an interval
key_conditions.evidence: the graph consists of line segments and no segment crosses the axis

verification.independent_path: numerical value and finite-difference slope of f' at each segment midpoint (independent of the sign table)

ap_calculus_ab-m17.stem: The graph of $f'$, the derivative of the function $f$, is shown for $0\le x\le 8$ and consists of line segments. How many points of inflection does the graph of $f$ have on the interval $0<x<8$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f', consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: f has an inflection point where f' changes from increasing to decreasing or from decreasing to increasing, which are the vertices where the slope of the graph of f' changes sign.
Counts the four line segments of the graph rather than the places where the direction of f' changes.
Counts every vertex of the graph of f' in (0, 8) as an inflection point of f.
Counts the zeros of f' (places where f may have an extremum) instead of the places where f' changes direction.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Locate points of inflection of f from the direction changes of the graph of f'
student_thinking: Recognize that concavity of f is determined by whether f' increases or decreases
Find the vertices where the slope of f' changes sign
Count those vertices on the interval

key_conditions.condition: f' is continuous so f is differentiable and a concavity change in f is a sign change of the slope of f'
key_conditions.evidence: the graph is a continuous polygon with nonzero slopes on every segment

verification.independent_path: dense sampling of the finite-difference slope of f' and counting its sign changes (independent of comparing segment slopes)

ap_calculus_ab-m18.stem: The graph of the function $f$, consisting of line segments, is shown. Let $F(x)=\int_0^{x^2} f(t)\,dt$. What is $F'(2)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: By the Fundamental Theorem with the chain rule, F'(x) = f(x^2) * 2x, so F'(2) = 2(2) f(4) with f(4) read from the graph.
Evaluates the integrand at x = 2 instead of at x^2 = 4.
Reports the value of the integral F(2), the area under f from 0 to 4, instead of F'(2).
Differentiates the integrand: 2x f'(x^2) instead of 2x f(x^2).

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Differentiate an accumulation function with an inner function in the upper limit using a graph of the integrand
student_thinking: Recognize F as an accumulation function with upper limit x squared
Apply the Fundamental Theorem with the chain rule: F' = f(x^2) 2x
Read f at the required input from the graph

key_conditions.condition: f is continuous so the Fundamental Theorem applies; the upper limit x^2 is differentiable
key_conditions.evidence: f is a continuous polygon graph

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of F computed by numerical quadrature of the interpolated graph (independent of the Fundamental Theorem)

ap_calculus_ab-m19.stem: Let $f(x)=e^{x/3}+x$, and let $g$ be the function whose graph, consisting of line segments, is shown. If $H(x)=f(x)+\int_0^x g(t)\,dt$, what is $H'(7)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Adds the area under g from 0 to 7, the value of the integral, instead of g(7).
Differentiates only f and treats the integral term as a constant.
Keeps only g(a) from the integral and forgets to differentiate f.
H'(x) = f'(x) + g(x) by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus; f'(a) is evaluated with a calculator and g(a) is read from the graph.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Differentiate a function that combines a formula and an accumulation of a graphed function
student_thinking: Differentiate the formula term and evaluate it at a with a calculator
Apply the Fundamental Theorem to the integral term to get g(a)
Read g(a) from the graph and add

key_conditions.condition: g is continuous so the Fundamental Theorem gives d/dx of the integral equal to g(x)
key_conditions.evidence: g is a continuous polygon graph

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of H built from the lambdified f and a quadrature of the interpolated g (independent of the Fundamental Theorem)

ap_calculus_ab-m20.stem: Water flows into a tank at a rate $I(t)$ and out at a rate $O(t)$, both in gallons per minute, for $0\le t\le 8$ minutes. The graphs of $I$ and $O$ are shown, and each consists of line segments. The tank holds 13 gallons at $t=0$. How many gallons are in the tank at $t=8$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of the inflow rate I and the outflow rate O, each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Amount at t = b equals the initial amount plus the integral of inflow minus outflow, each area read from the graphs.
Adds the outflow instead of subtracting it.
Counts only the water that flows in.
Subtracts the inflow from the outflow, reversing the net change.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Use net change of inflow minus outflow from two rate graphs and the initial amount
student_thinking: Recognize the amount at time b as initial amount plus the integral of (inflow - outflow)
Compute the area under each graph from 0 to b
Combine initial amount, inflow area and outflow area

key_conditions.condition: amount at time b = initial amount + integral of the net rate
key_conditions.evidence: net change theorem; both rates are given for the whole interval

verification.independent_path: numerical quadrature of the two interpolated rate graphs (independent of the trapezoid formula)

ap_calculus_ab-m21.stem: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{1+\frac{x^{3}}{30}}$. The graph of the function $g$, which consists of line segments, is shown for $0\le x\le 8$. What is the value of $\int_0^8\left(f(x)+2g(x)\right)dx$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Split the integral: the integral of f needs a calculator, and 2 times the integral of g is 2 times the area under the graph.
Subtracts 2 times the area of g instead of adding it.
Leaves out the coefficient 2 on g and adds the plain area of g.
Evaluates only the integral of f and ignores g.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Use linearity of the definite integral when one function is a formula and the other is a graph
student_thinking: Split the integral of a sum into two integrals and pull out the constant
Evaluate the integral of f numerically with a calculator
Evaluate the integral of g as the area read from the graph, then combine

key_conditions.condition: the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals and constants factor out
key_conditions.evidence: linearity of the definite integral

verification.independent_path: composite Simpson rule (20001 nodes) on f + c g with g interpolated (independent of the split into two integrals)

ap_calculus_ab-m22.stem: The graph of the function $f$ is shown. It consists of two line segments and a semicircle. What is the value of $\int_0^8 f(x)\,dx$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f: a line segment, a semicircle with diameter on the x-axis, and a line segment below the axis.

options.why: Leaves out the semicircle and adds only the two triangles.
The integral is the signed area: the left triangle, plus the semicircle of area (1/2) pi r^2, minus the triangle below the x-axis.
Uses the area of a full circle, pi r^2, for the semicircle.
Treats the triangle below the x-axis as positive area instead of negative.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Evaluate a definite integral as signed area using geometric shapes read from a graph
student_thinking: Identify the shapes (two triangles and a semicircle) and read their dimensions from the graph
Use geometric area formulas, counting area below the axis as negative
Add the signed areas

key_conditions.condition: the definite integral equals the signed area between the graph and the x-axis
key_conditions.evidence: geometric interpretation of the integral for a piecewise geometric graph

must_include: segment from (0, y0) to the left end of the semicircle
segment below the axis to x = 8

misconceptions.description: counts the area below the axis as positive

verification.independent_path: numerical quadrature of the explicit piecewise formula with the sqrt semicircle (independent of the geometric area formulas)

ap_calculus_ab-m23.stem: The graph of the one-to-one function $f$, which consists of line segments, is shown. Let $g$ be the inverse function of $f$. What is $g'(5)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Takes the reciprocal of the function value, 1/f(3) = 1/5, instead of the reciprocal of the slope.
g'(b) = 1 / f'(g(b)). Here f(3) = 5, so g(5) = 3 and g'(5) is the reciprocal of the slope of f at x = 3.
Reports f'(a) itself instead of its reciprocal.
Takes the negative reciprocal -1/f'(a).

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Differentiate an inverse function at a point using the graph of the original function
student_thinking: Find the x-value a with f(a) = b from the graph
Read the slope of f at x = a
Take the reciprocal to get the derivative of the inverse

key_conditions.condition: f is increasing, hence one-to-one, and differentiable at a because a is interior to a segment
key_conditions.evidence: vertices are strictly increasing; a is odd

verification.independent_path: numerical inverse by Brent's method on the interpolated graph, then a central difference of that inverse (independent of the reciprocal rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m24.stem: The graphs of the differentiable functions $f$ and $g$ are shown, each consisting of line segments, and both graphs pass through $(7,0)$. What is $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 7}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of f and g, each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: The quotient has the form 0/0 at x = a, so the limit equals f'(a)/g'(a), the ratio of the slopes read from the graphs (L'Hopital's Rule).
Substitutes x = 7 and concludes the quotient 0/0 equals 0.
Takes the ratio of slopes upside down, g'(a)/f'(a).
Multiplies the two slopes instead of dividing them.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Evaluate a 0/0 limit by comparing the slopes of two graphs at their common zero
student_thinking: Check that f(a) = g(a) = 0 so the limit is indeterminate 0/0
Choose L'Hopital's Rule and read the two slopes at x = a
Form the ratio f'(a)/g'(a)

key_conditions.condition: f and g are differentiable at a with g'(a) not zero, so L'Hopital's Rule applies
key_conditions.evidence: both graphs are lines near x = a and the slope of g is nonzero

verification.independent_path: evaluating the interpolated quotient f/g at x = a +/- 1e-7 (independent of the slope ratio)

ap_calculus_ab-m25.stem: The graph of the function $f$ is shown. What is the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^-}f(x)+\lim_{x\to 3^+}f(x)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f: two line segments with open circles at x = 3 and a separate filled point at x = 3.

options.why: The left-hand limit is -1 and the right-hand limit is 4 (open circles show the values approached); the plotted value f(3) = 1 does not enter the one-sided limits.
Multiplies the one-sided limits instead of adding them.
Subtracts the right-hand limit from the left-hand limit.
Adds f(3) to the left-hand limit and ignores the right-hand limit.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Read one-sided limits from a graph with a jump and an isolated plotted value
student_thinking: Read the value approached from the left, ignoring the plotted point
Read the value approached from the right
Add the two limits

key_conditions.condition: one-sided limits are determined by the graph near x = c, not by f(c)
key_conditions.evidence: open circles mark the limit values and a separate filled point marks f(c)

must_include: left piece ending at an open circle at x = c
right piece starting at an open circle at x = c

verification.independent_path: numerical evaluation of the two linear pieces at c -/+ 1e-9 (independent of the endpoints read from the figure)

ap_calculus_ab-m26.stem: The figure shows the graph of $f(x)=3xe^{-x/2}$ for $0\le x\le 6$ and the line $L$. At what value of $x$ in the interval $(0,6)$ is the tangent line to the graph of $f$ parallel to $L$?

stimulus.description: Graph of the curve y = f(x) and the line L.

options.why: Solves f'(x) = 1, treating the y-intercept of the line as its slope.
Read the slope of L from the figure, then solve f'(x) = slope numerically with a calculator.
Solves f(x) equal to the slope of L instead of f'(x) equal to the slope.
Finds where the curve crosses the line, f(x) = L(x), instead of where the slopes are equal.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find where the tangent to a curve is parallel to a line whose slope is read from a graph
student_thinking: Read two lattice points on L from the figure and find its slope
Differentiate f and set f'(x) equal to the slope of L
Solve the equation numerically with a calculator

key_conditions.condition: parallel lines have equal slopes and f' has exactly one solution of f'(x) = slope on (0, 6)
key_conditions.evidence: f'(x) = A(1 - x/2)e^{-x/2} is monotonic on the relevant branch for 0 < slope < A

must_include: line L through two lattice points

misconceptions.description: uses the intercept as the slope

verification.independent_path: bisection on the central-difference derivative with 100 halvings (independent of the symbolic derivative and Brent's method)

ap_calculus_ab-m27.stem: Let $f(x)=e^{x/3}+x$. The graph of the function $g$, which consists of line segments, is shown. If $h(x)=f(x)\,g(x)$, what is the value of $h'(3)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Evaluates the product f(a) g(a) and does not differentiate.
Keeps only the first product rule term f'(a) g(a).
h'(a) = f'(a) g(a) + f(a) g'(a); g(a) and g'(a) come from the graph and f'(a), f(a) from the formula (calculator).
Keeps only the second product rule term f(a) g'(a).

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Apply the product rule at a point when one factor is a formula and the other is a graph
student_thinking: Differentiate the formula and evaluate f(a), f'(a) with a calculator
Read g(a) and the slope g'(a) from the graph of g
Combine them with the product rule

key_conditions.condition: g is differentiable at x = a because a is interior to a segment of its graph
key_conditions.evidence: a is an odd integer and the vertices of g are at even x

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of the product of the lambdified formula and the interpolated graph (independent of the product rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m28.stem: The graphs of the functions $f$ and $g$ are shown; each consists of line segments. Let $h(x)=f(x)\,g(x)$. What is $h'(3)$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of f and g, each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Multiplies the two derivatives, f'(a) g'(a), instead of using the product rule.
Keeps only the second product rule term f(a) g'(a).
h'(a) = f'(a) g(a) + f(a) g'(a), using the values and slopes read from the segments containing x = 3.
Keeps only the first product rule term f'(a) g(a).

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Apply the product rule at a point using values and slopes read from two graphs
student_thinking: Read f(a), g(a) and the slopes of the segments containing x = a
Apply the product rule h' = f' g + f g'
Evaluate with the values read from the graphs

key_conditions.condition: f and g are differentiable at x = a because a lies inside a segment of each graph
key_conditions.evidence: x = a is not a vertex of either graph

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of the product of the numerically interpolated graphs (independent of the product rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m29.stem: The functions $f$ and $g$ have the graphs shown, each made of line segments. If $q(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$, find $q'(1)$.

stimulus.description: Graphs of f and g, each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: q'(a) = (f'(a) g(a) - f(a) g'(a)) / g(a)^2 with values and slopes read from the graphs.
Divides the derivatives, f'(a)/g'(a), instead of using the quotient rule.
Adds the two terms of the numerator instead of subtracting them.
Reverses the order of the numerator: f g' - f' g.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Apply the quotient rule at a point using values and slopes read from two graphs
student_thinking: Read f(a), g(a) and the two slopes from the segments containing x = a
Apply the quotient rule with the numerator in the correct order
Simplify the resulting fraction

key_conditions.condition: g(a) is not zero and both graphs are linear near x = a
key_conditions.evidence: g(a) read from the graph is nonzero; a is interior to a segment of each graph

misconceptions.description: divides by g instead of g squared

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of the numerically interpolated quotient (independent of the quotient rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m30.stem: The radius $r(t)$ and the height $h(t)$, in centimeters, of a right circular cone at time $t$ seconds are shown in the graphs, each consisting of line segments. The volume of the cone is $V=\frac13\pi r^2h$. At what rate, in cubic centimeters per second, is the volume changing at $t=5$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of r(t) and h(t), each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Evaluates V itself, (pi/3) r^2 h, instead of dV/dt.
Forgets the factor 1/3 in the volume formula.
Omits the h'(t) term of the product rule and keeps only (pi/3)(2 r h r').
dV/dt = (pi/3)(2 r h r' + r^2 h') with r, h, r', h' read from the graphs at t = 5.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Solve a related rates problem for a cone when both dimensions are given by graphs
student_thinking: Differentiate V = (1/3) pi r^2 h with respect to t using the product and chain rules
Read r, h, r' and h' at the given time from the graphs
Substitute and simplify

key_conditions.condition: r and h are differentiable at the given time because it lies inside a segment of each graph
key_conditions.evidence: t is an odd integer, never a vertex

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of V(t) built from the numerically interpolated r and h (independent of the product rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m31.stem: The graph of the function $f$, consisting of line segments, is shown. A left Riemann sum with 4 subintervals of equal length is used to approximate $\int_0^8 f(x)\,dx$. What is the value of this approximation?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: The width is 2 and the left endpoints are x = 0, 2, 4, 6, so the sum is 2 [f(0) + f(2) + f(4) + f(6)] using values read from the graph.
Adds all five vertex values f(0), f(2), f(4), f(6), f(8), which is one more value than a 4-subinterval left sum uses.
Uses right endpoints f(2), f(4), f(6), f(8) instead of left endpoints.
Adds the four left-endpoint values and forgets to multiply by the subinterval width 2.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Compute a left Riemann sum using function values read from a graph
student_thinking: Find the subinterval width and the left endpoints
Read f at each left endpoint from the graph
Multiply the sum of values by the width

key_conditions.condition: the 4 subintervals have equal length 2 and left endpoints 0, 2, 4, 6
key_conditions.evidence: stated by the problem; all four endpoints are vertices of the graph

verification.independent_path: direct sum of the numerically interpolated function at the left endpoints times 2 (independent of exact vertex arithmetic)

ap_calculus_ab-m32.stem: A particle moves along a straight line with velocity $v(t)$ meters per second for $0\le t\le 8$. The graph of $v$ is shown and consists of line segments. On which of the following time intervals is the speed of the particle increasing?

stimulus.description: Graph of v(t), consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign: on this interval v and the slope of v are both negative.
On (6, 8) the velocity is negative and increasing toward zero, so the speed is decreasing.
On (0, 2) the velocity is negative and increasing toward zero, so the speed is decreasing.
On (2, 4) the velocity is negative and increasing toward zero, so the speed is decreasing.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Decide when speed increases from the graph of velocity
student_thinking: Read the sign of v and the slope of v on each segment
Speed increases exactly when velocity and acceleration have the same sign
Select the interval where this holds

key_conditions.condition: acceleration is the slope of the velocity graph and is constant on each segment
key_conditions.evidence: the graph consists of line segments

verification.independent_path: numerical |v| at t = midpoint +/- 0.01 on every segment (independent of the sign table)

ap_calculus_ab-m33.stem: The function $f$ is differentiable and $f(1)=3$. The graph of $f'$, consisting of line segments, is shown. The tangent line to the graph of $f$ at $x=1$ is used to approximate $f(2)$. Which of the following gives the approximation and describes how it compares with $f(2)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f', consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: The tangent line at x = 1 uses slope f'(1) = -1, giving f(1) + f'(1); f' is decreasing there, so f is concave down and the tangent line lies above the graph.
Uses the slope at the right endpoint x = 2 and also reverses the concavity argument.
Computes the correct tangent value but reverses the concavity argument: f' is decreasing, so f is concave down.
Uses the slope at the right endpoint x = 2 instead of the slope at x = 1.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Use the tangent line at a point to approximate a value and decide over/under estimate from the graph of f'
student_thinking: Read f'(a) from the graph and form the tangent line approximation f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)
Decide concavity of f from whether f' is increasing or decreasing near x = a
State whether the tangent line value is below or above the true value

key_conditions.condition: f' is linear on (a - 1, a + 1) with nonzero slope, so f is strictly concave up or down there
key_conditions.evidence: a is interior to a segment of the f' graph whose slope is nonzero

misconceptions.description: uses the slope at x = a + 1

verification.independent_path: numerical integral of f' over [a, a+1] gives the true f(a+1); the sign of true - tangent value is compared with the claim

ap_calculus_ab-m34.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity $v(t)$ in meters per second. The graph of $v$ for $0\le t\le 8$ is shown and consists of line segments. The particle's position at $t=0$ is $x(0)=5$ meters. What is the total distance traveled by the particle from $t=0$ to $t=8$?

stimulus.description: Graph of v(t), consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Counts only the forward motion (area above the axis) and ignores the backward motion.
Total distance is the integral of |v|: the area between the graph and the t-axis, with area below the axis counted as positive.
Reports the net signed area, which is the displacement, not the distance.
Reports the particle's final position x(8) = x(0) + displacement.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Distinguish total distance from displacement and final position using a velocity graph
student_thinking: Recognize that total distance is the integral of speed |v|, not of v
Find the areas above and below the axis separately from the graph
Add the magnitudes

key_conditions.condition: distance traveled is the integral of |v| over the interval
key_conditions.evidence: definition of total distance for straight-line motion

verification.independent_path: numerical quadrature of |v| with breakpoints at the vertices (independent of the exact piecewise formula)

ap_calculus_ab-m35.stem: The graph of the function $f$ is shown and consists of line segments. Let $R$ be the region bounded by the graph of $f$, the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines $x=0$ and $x=8$. $R$ is the base of a solid whose cross sections perpendicular to the $x$-axis are squares. What is the volume of the solid?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Uses half of the integral of f squared, the area formula for a right-triangle cross section.
Squares the area of the base region, (integral of f)^2, instead of integrating f squared.
Multiplies the integral of f squared by pi, the formula for rotating the region about the x-axis.
Each square has side f(x), so V = integral of f(x)^2 dx; on a linear piece the integral of f^2 is (a^2 + a b + b^2)/3 times the width.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Set up and evaluate a volume with square cross sections whose side is given by a graph
student_thinking: Recognize that the side of each square is f(x) and its area is f(x) squared
Integrate f squared over [0, 8] piece by piece using the graph
Evaluate the exact value

key_conditions.condition: f is nonnegative so the side length equals f(x)
key_conditions.evidence: all plotted vertices are at or above the x-axis

misconceptions.description: halves the integral of f squared

verification.independent_path: numerical quadrature of the interpolated f squared (independent of the exact quadratic piece formula)

ap_calculus_ab-m36.stem: The figure shows the graph of $f(x)=3xe^{-x/2}$ and the line $L$. Let $R$ be the region enclosed by the graph of $f$ and the line $L$. $R$ is the base of a solid whose cross sections perpendicular to the $x$-axis are squares. What is the volume of the solid?

stimulus.description: Graph of the curve y = f(x) and the line L; the region R between them is described in the problem.

options.why: Reports the area of R and does not square the side length.
The side of each square is f(x) - L(x) between the intersection points, so V = integral of (f - L)^2 evaluated with a calculator.
Integrates the difference of squares, f^2 - L^2, instead of the square of the difference.
Squares the area of R, (integral of f - L)^2, instead of integrating the squared side length.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find the volume of a solid with square cross sections whose base is bounded by a curve and a graphed line
student_thinking: Read the line from the figure and find the intersection points with a calculator
Set the side length of each square equal to the vertical distance f - L
Integrate the square of that distance between the intersection points

key_conditions.condition: the cross sections are squares with side f - L because f is above L between the intersection points
key_conditions.evidence: shown in the figure

must_include: line L through two lattice points

verification.independent_path: composite Simpson rule on (f - L)^2 between Brent-found roots (independent of scipy quad)

ap_calculus_ab-m37.stem: The figure shows the graph of $f(x)=4\sin x$ and the line $L$. Let $R$ be the region enclosed by the graph of $f$ and the line $L$. $R$ is revolved about the $x$-axis. What is the volume of the solid generated?

stimulus.description: Graph of the curve y = f(x) and the line L; the region R between them is described in the problem.

options.why: Uses only the outer radius f, as a disk with no hole.
Washers with outer radius f(x) and inner radius L(x): V = pi times the integral of (f^2 - L^2) between the intersection points, evaluated with a calculator.
Leaves out the factor pi.
Squares the difference of the radii, pi times the integral of (f - L)^2, instead of the difference of the squared radii.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Find a washer-method volume for a region bounded by a curve and a graphed line, revolved about the x-axis
student_thinking: Read the line from the figure and find the intersection points with a calculator
Identify the outer radius f and the inner radius L
Integrate pi (f^2 - L^2) between the intersection points

key_conditions.condition: the region lies above the x-axis and f >= L > 0 between the intersection points, so washers are formed
key_conditions.evidence: shown in the figure; both y-intercepts are nonnegative

must_include: line L through two lattice points

verification.independent_path: composite Simpson rule on pi (f^2 - L^2) between Brent-found roots (independent of scipy quad)
